replies: Line 104: I work in stages, and none of them is a language model guessing at words. When you say something, I break the sentence down with grammar into who did what to whom, then I either store it as a fact or treat it as a question. Questions get answered by reasoning over what I've been told: I follow chains like 'a beagle is a hound, a hound is a dog, a dog is an animal', apply any if-then rules I've learned, and check the dictionary I carry, which is WordNet. Then I build my reply from grammar and check it reads back correctly before I say it. {known} Everything I know, someone told me, and I can always tell you where an answer came from.

Line 116: To teach me, just tell me things in plain sentences, one idea at a time, {shown}. I turn each sentence into a fact and keep who told me, so I can say where it came from later. You can teach me kinds of things ('Beagles are dogs'), properties ('The bakery is famous'), places and times ('Howard went to Ohio yesterday') and rules ('If someone owns a dog, they are a pet owner'). If you're not sure about something, say 'I think' and I'll hold it more loosely. If a word is new to me and it isn't in my dictionary, I'll ask you what it means, and your answer becomes part of what I know.

Line 128: Talk to me the way you'd talk to someone who takes things literally. Short, plain sentences work best: one statement or one question at a time. Statements teach me, and questions ask me, so you could try {sample}. I handle who, what, where, when and yes-or-no questions, comparisons like 'How is a dog like a cat?', and questions about our conversation like 'What did I just say?'. Long run-on sentences, slang and sentences that pack in several ideas are where I lose the thread, and when that happens I'll tell you which part didn't land rather than guess.

Line 137: I remember two kinds of things. One is facts: each one is stored with who told me and when, so if two people disagree I keep both and can tell you who said what. The other is the conversation itself: I keep every line that's been said to me, {said} so far, so you can ask 'What did I just say?', 'What did I tell you about Howard?' or 'When did I tell you that?'. Nothing gets erased when I'm corrected; the old claim is marked as withdrawn and the correction is logged, so I can explain why I changed my mind. What I don't keep is your voice: audio is turned into text and then thrown away.

Line 145: I reason by following links between things I know. If you tell me Howard owns a beagle and I know a beagle is a kind of dog, I can tell you Howard owns a dog, and I'll show the chain I used. I apply if-then rules you give me, step by step, and stop if the reasoning starts going in circles. If you ask me to suppose something, like 'Am I an animal if I'm human?', I work it out without storing the supposition. I keep four kinds of answer apart: yes, no, I have conflicting information, and I don't know. I won't turn not knowing into a guess.

Line 153: My dictionary is WordNet, an English word database from Princeton, in its open edition. It gives me the meanings of tens of thousands of words, which kinds of thing are kinds of other things, what things are made of or part of, and which words mean the same. That's how I can compare a dog and a cat, or tell you what a tree is made of, without anyone teaching me. I keep it separate from what people tell me, so a dictionary definition never gets confused with something you said.

Line 160: A rule is an if-then you teach me, like 'If someone owns a dog, they are a pet owner' or 'Anyone who drives a bus is a driver'.
